evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental results.

claim: The gene duplication that created PIC2 and MIR1 was an ancient event.
source: Our phylogenetic analyses of PIC2 and MIR1 sequences suggest that the gene duplication that created these two orthologs was an ancient event
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The loss of MIR1 has occurred multiple times in eukaryotes.
source: The loss of MIR1 has occurred multiple times in eukaryotes, an event that is likely facilitated by the dual specificity of PIC2.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: SLC25A3 is essential in mammals as the homozygous deletion is embryonic lethal.
source: SLC25A3 is essential in mammals as the homozygous deletion is embryonic lethal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Mammals express two SLC25A3 isoforms: isoform A is expressed primarily in heart and skeletal muscle whereas isoform B is expressed in all tissues.
source: While mammals do express two SLC25A3 isoforms, isoform A is expressed primarily in heart and skeletal muscle whereas isoform B is expressed in all tissues (Fiermonte et al., 1998; Seifert et al., 2016; Kwong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: COX17 has dual localization in cytosol and IMS.
source: The recruitment of Cu to mitochondria was initially attributed to COX17 due to its dual localization in cytosol and IMS (Glerum et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: COX is fully functional when COX17 is artificially restricted to the IMS by an IM tether.
source: However, COX is fully functional when COX17 is artificially restricted to the IMS by an IM tether (Maxfield et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Yeast cells lacking COX17 accumulate wild-type levels of Cu in mitochondria.
source: Consistent with a mitochondrially restricted function for COX17 in Cu handling, yeast cells lacking this gene accumulate wild-type levels of Cu in mitochondria (Cobine et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: A non-proteinaceous ligand (CuL) accumulates in the mitochondrial matrix.
source: In fact, attempts to isolate a protein that delivers Cu to mitochondria led to the identification of a non-proteinaceous ligand (CuL) that accumulates in the matrix (Cobine et al., 2021; Vest et al., 2019; Vest and Cobine, 2011; Cobine et al., 2006; Cobine et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: PIC2 is able to transport both the CuL purified from the mitochondrial matrix as well as ionic Cu in both liposomes and the L. lactis system.
source: PIC2 is able to transport both the CuL purified from the mitochondrial matrix as well as ionic Cu in both liposomes and the L. lactis system (Vest et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The ionic Cu in transport assays is Cu+ due to the presence of an exogenous reductant or the endogenous reductant menaquinone in L. lactis.
source: The ionic Cu in our transport assays is Cu+ due to the presence of an exogenous reductant (e.g., ascorbate) or the endogenous reductant menaquinone in L. lactis (Abicht et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: In the L175A mutation of SLC25A3, the COX defect in mutant cells is due to defective Cu transport rather than reduced phosphate levels.
source: This finding confirms that the COX defect in mutant cells is due to defective Cu transport rather than reduced phosphate levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental results with the L175A mutant.

claim: Compromising the phosphate transport function of PIC2 is easier than inactivating its Cu transport function.
source: Further, our data suggest that compromising the phosphate transport function of PIC2 is easier than inactivating its Cu transport function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the mutagenesis results.

claim: Mutations in a series of cysteine and histidine residues lining the aqueous binding pocket of the c-state model decrease, but do not eliminate, Cu transport.
source: Mutations in a series of cysteine and histidine residues lining the aqueous binding pocket of the c-state model decrease, but do not eliminate, Cu transport.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the mutagenesis results.

claim: The CuL complex has a net negative charge.
source: To understand the transport of the CuL complex, we considered the net negative charge of the complex
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: NMR analysis of the CuL shows the presence of an aromatic ring structure.
source: NMR analysis of the CuL by proton and carbon spectrums shows the presence of an aromatic ring structure with proton chemical shifts of 6.5–8 ppm and carbon chemical shifts of 110–175 ppm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ring structure of CuL is consistent with the fluorescent properties of the CuL complex.
source: The ring structure is consistent with the fluorescent properties of the CuL complex (Vest et al., 2013; Cobine et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Nine taxa lack a PIC2-like ortholog but have retained COX.
source: Our phylogenetic analysis revealed nine taxa that lack a PIC2-like ortholog but have retained COX.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Each of the nine taxa that lack PIC2 have multiple MIR1-like transporters.
source: Each of these taxa have multiple MIR1-like transporters (Guillardia theta, Thalassiosira pseudonana, Emiliania huxleyi, Dictyostelium discoideum, Ustilago maydis, Cyanidioschyzon merolae, Chrysochromulina tobinii, Micromonas commoda, and Naegleria gruberi).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: In yeast, MRS3 serves as a secondary importer of mitochondrial Cu.
source: Indeed, in yeast we have shown that the MCF family member MRS3 serves as a secondary importer of mitochondrial Cu (Vest et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: MRS3 is known as an iron transporter.
source: MRS3 is known as an iron transporter, but transport of Cu by MRS3 and its orthologs has been reported in studies using mitochondrially derived vesicles from yeast and plants and in a reconstituted assay system (Brazzolotto et al., 2014; Froschauer et al., 2009; Christenson et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Transport of Cu by MRS3 and its orthologs has been reported in studies using mitochondrially derived vesicles from yeast and plants and in a reconstituted assay system.
source: but transport of Cu by MRS3 and its orthologs has been reported in studies using mitochondrially derived vesicles from yeast and plants and in a reconstituted assay system (Brazzolotto et al., 2014; Froschauer et al., 2009; Christenson et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Lys90, Leu127, and Met275 are important for phosphate transport but are dispensable for Cu transport in L. lactis.
source: Our biochemical data suggest that Lys90, Leu127, and Met275 are important for phosphate transport but are dispensable for Cu transport in L. lactis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the mutagenesis results.

claim: Leu127 is located on helix 3 adjacent to a proline that kinks the helix.
source: The PIC2 structural model shows that Leu127 is located on helix 3 adjacent to a proline that kinks the helix, thereby altering helix–helix packing interactions with helix 2 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 8.

claim: The Leu127 side chain interacts with the peptide backbone between Leu85 and Gln86 in a knobs-into-holes interaction.
source: The Leu127 side chain interacts with the peptide backbone between Leu85 (Met in SLC25A3) and Gln86 in a knobs-into-holes interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on structural modeling.

claim: Cu transport requires the formation of transient covalent bonds between the metal and ligands during transport.
source: Cu transport requires the formation of transient covalent bonds between the metal and ligands during transport, whereas phosphate transport relies on hydrogen bonding and salt bridges.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Phosphate transport relies on hydrogen bonding and salt bridges.
source: Cu transport requires the formation of transient covalent bonds between the metal and ligands during transport, whereas phosphate transport relies on hydrogen bonding and salt bridges.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Mitochondria function as a metabolic hub that controls physiology and disease by balancing the concentrations of multiple metabolites and essential elements.
source: Mitochondria function as a metabolic hub that controls physiology and disease by balancing the concentrations of multiple metabolites and essential elements (Baker et al., 2017; Martínez-Reyes and Chandel, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: MCF proteins play a critical role in regulating the import and export of substrates in mitochondria.
source: The MCF proteins play a critical role in regulating the import and export of these substrates (Cunningham and Rutter, 2020; Palmieri et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Storage of Cu in the mitochondrial matrix may have evolved as a mechanism to ensure Cu availability for COX assembly in an early endosymbiont.
source: Storage in the mitochondrial matrix may have evolved as a mechanism to ensure Cu availability for COX assembly in an early endosymbiont that was subsequently retained during eukaryogenesis (Cobine et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Mitochondrial Cu can induce cell death through a pathway coined cuproptosis.
source: The recent discoveries that mitochondrial Cu can induce cell death through a pathway coined cuproptosis (Tsvetkov et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Mitochondrial Cu can disrupt essential processes such as Fe–S assembly.
source: disrupt essential processes such as Fe–S assembly (Vallières et al., 2017; Brancaccio et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondrial Cu can alter the stability of SOD1 in the cytosol.
source: and alter the stability of SOD1 in the cytosol (Boulet et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.
